prompt: Which is a good SLI for the shop's API?

choices.text: CPU use of the Cloud Run instances
choices.why: Nobody experiences CPU; they experience failed or slow requests.

choices.text: The share of requests with no 5xx
choices.why: Right. A ratio of good events, as the user sees them.

choices.text: The number of instances running
choices.why: A count of machines says nothing about the user.

choices.text: The number of deployments this week
choices.why: That is a delivery metric, not service quality.

prompt: The API is down and requests never reach it. Where must the SLI be measured to count them as failures?
hint: Inside the API, they are not seen at all.

choices.text: Inside the API, in its own code
choices.why: A dead API counts nothing; the SLI looks perfect.

choices.text: In front of the API
choices.why: Right. That is where request_count is measured.

choices.text: In the database
choices.why: The database never sees requests that did not arrive.

choices.text: In Error Reporting
choices.why: It groups errors that were logged, which these were not.

prompt: What separates an SLO from an SLA?

choices.text: An SLA is measured over a shorter window
choices.why: Windows vary; the difference is the promise.

choices.text: An SLO is written in percent and an SLA in minutes
choices.why: Either can be written either way.

choices.text: An SLA carries a customer consequence
choices.why: Right. And the SLO is set tighter, to notice first.

choices.text: An SLO applies only to latency
choices.why: Any SLI can have an SLO.

prompt: A service handles 1,000,000 requests in its window with a 99.5% SLO. How many requests is its error budget?
What does a burn rate of 1 mean?
hint: Compared with the pace the target allows.

choices.text: One request failed
choices.why: A rate is a ratio, not a count.

choices.text: The budget is used up
choices.why: That is the state after a burn, not its pace.

choices.text: The budget would last exactly the window
choices.why: Right. Below 1 saves budget; above 1 spends it early.

choices.text: 1% of requests are failing
choices.why: For a 99.5% target that would be a burn rate of 2.

prompt: Day 19 burned at 4.77 on average over the day. What does that average hide?
hint: The failures came in one afternoon.

choices.text: A few hours that burned far faster than that
choices.why: Right. A daily number spreads a bad afternoon over 24 hours.

choices.text: That the SLO was missed that day
choices.why: The SLO is over 28 days, and was met.

choices.text: A burn rate below 1 for the rest of the month
choices.why: Those days are shown separately; the average hides nothing about them.

choices.text: Nothing: the average is the whole story
choices.why: Averages flatten peaks, exactly as lesson 8 showed.

prompt: With 5% of the error budget left, what does the shop do?

choices.text: Raise the target to 99.9% to compensate
choices.why: A tighter target with no budget is a target already missed.

choices.text: Freeze risky releases for a while
choices.why: Right. Until the window rolls past the bad days.

choices.text: Nothing until the first of next month
choices.why: The window is rolling; there is no monthly reset.

choices.text: Ship faster to use the rest
choices.why: 5% left is the signal to slow down.

prompt: With a 28-day rolling window, on which day do day 19's failures stop counting against the budget?
Why alert on the burn rate rather than on the SLI over five minutes?
hint: A blip, or a real spend?

choices.text: Burn rates are cheaper to compute
choices.why: Cost is not the reason.

choices.text: It pages only for real risk
choices.why: Right. A five-minute SLI pages on every blip.

choices.text: Cloud Monitoring cannot alert on an SLI
choices.why: It can; it is just the wrong question.

choices.text: The SLI is only known at the end of the window
choices.why: It is computed continuously.

prompt: Why does the fast-burn policy also need the 5-minute condition, joined by AND?

choices.text: To catch incidents shorter than five minutes
choices.why: With AND, a short spike alone does not fire.

choices.text: Because one condition per policy is not allowed
choices.why: One condition is allowed.

choices.text: So an incident that already ended does not keep paging
choices.why: Right. The hour's average stays high after the fix; the five minutes do not.

choices.text: To double the threshold to 28.8
choices.why: Both conditions use 14.4; nothing doubles.

prompt: A burn rate of 14.4 lasts one hour against a 28-day (672-hour) window. What percentage of the whole budget is spent?
The function a condition uses to read an SLO's burn rate is `select_slo____`.
hint: Two words joined by underscores, after slo.

prompt: Match each term to the shop's value.
hint: One right-hand value belongs to none.

pairs.right: none: the shop sells no guarantee

prompt: Put the building of the shop's SLO in order.
hint: Decide what is good before setting a target for it.
items: Decide what a good request is
Set the target and the window
trap: Setting 99.5% before deciding what counts as good is the slip: the number would measure nothing yet.
